content.content:
# Floorplan **See how your app actually fits together.** Claude or Codex reads your codebase and draws an interactive map of it. Every part, file and web request gets a plain-English name, and every connection between them is shown. [![Claude Code plugin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude%20Code-plugin-D97757?style=flat-square)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview) [![Codex plugin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Codex-plugin-111?style=flat-square)](docs/codex.md) [![Tests](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/haydenschmitty/floorplan/test.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=tests)](https://github.com/haydenschmitty/floorplan/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.6.1-111?style=flat-square)](CHANGELOG.md) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-111?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Node 18+](https://img.shields.io/badge/node-%E2%89%A518-111?style=flat-square)](https://nodejs.org) [![Zero dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-0-111?style=flat-square)](#how-it-works) **[Try the live demo](https://haydenschmitty.github.io/floorplan-demo/)** · [Watch the video](https://youtu.be/NTUUzC7L_NQ) · [Install](#install) · [Quick start](#quick-start) · [Compared](#floorplan-archify-or-understand-anything) · [Features](#features) · [See it in action](#see-it-in-action) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Docs](docs/README.md) · [FAQ](#faq)

▶ Watch the walkthrough: installing Floorplan, then a tour of Brewline, a demo coffee-subscription app built across four repos.

Try the live demo → Explore the Brewline map in your browser, no install needed.

## Why Floorplan? You built an app, probably with a lot of help from AI, and it works. But ask "what happens when someone checks out?" or "what breaks if I change this?" and the honest answer is *no idea*. Floorplan gives you the diagram nobody drew. Ask Claude Code or Codex for a floorplan and a few minutes later you have a map you can explore, ask questions on, and keep up to date as you work. - **For builders:** understand the app you made, in your own words, without reading the code. - **For teams:** onboard someone in minutes, from the big picture down to the exact file. - **For working with AI:** after every change Claude or Codex makes, see exactly which parts it touched and why. ## Floorplan, Archify or Understand Anything? All three turn code into something you can see, and all three are worth knowing. They answer different questions: | | **Floorplan** | **[Archify](https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify)** | **[Understand Anything](https://github.com/Egonex-AI/Understand-Anything)** | |---|---|---|---| | **The question it answers** | How does the app I built actually work, and what should I worry about? | How do I show this clearly? | How does this big codebase work, down to the functions? | | **Made for** | People who build with AI and don't read the code | Anyone explaining a system, a process or an idea | Developers getting to know a large codebase | | **What you get** | A zoomable map of your whole app: parts, files and endpoints, the screens, the requests between frontend and backend (even across repos), and outside services | A polished diagram in one of 10 types (architecture, sequence, ERD…) or a one-page explainer, from a repo or just a description | A knowledge graph of every file, function and class, with layers, a business-domain view | **Only here** | **Health check** (keys in code, open Supabase tables and Firebase rules, fakeable Stripe webhooks, endpoints anyone can use), **Recent work** (what your AI just changed, and why), blueprints from a PRD | 10 diagram types, image and video exports, diagrams of things that aren't code | Diff impact, a dashboard that adapts to your role, knowledge-base graphs | | **Runs in** | Claude Code, Codex | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and more | Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI and more | **Pick Floorplan** to understand and check an app you own. **Pick Archify** to draw a diagram for a doc, a talk or a decision. **Pick Understand Anything** to study a large codebase function by function. They also work together: map your app with Floorplan, then use Archify to draw one flow for a presentation. ## Features
**🗺️ A map at every zoom**
Start with the whole app, then double-click into a part, a group of files, a file, and its endpoints. Each view shows what it's used by and what it uses. 		**💬 Plain English everywhere**
"Takes card payments at checkout", not "Stripe API wrapper". Technical terms are explained on hover, and one switch shows the developer view.
**🔌 Real connections, across repos**
It follows imports, and matches each web request in your frontend to the server endpoint that answers it, even across separate repos. 		**🖥️ Start from a screen**
Pick a page you know and see everything behind it: its parts, the requests it makes, the server code, the data, and outside services.
**🧭 Ask the map**
"How does a refund reach the customer's card?" comes back as an answer plus a mini-map of just the pieces involved, with a step-by-step walkthrough. 		**🩺 Health check**
Catches the classic mistakes in AI-built apps: keys in the code or sent to the browser, Supabase tables anyone can read, open Firebase rules, Stripe webhooks anyone could fake, and endpoints with no sign-in. Each comes with a ready-to-paste fix. A check, not an audit.
**🟢 Recent work**
The cards your AI just changed light up green, each with a note on how the change serves what you asked for. 		**⚡ Stays current, stays yours**
Updates re-read only what changed, and an open map reloads itself. Everything runs on your machine, and nothing is committed to git.
Plus guided **flows** you can request in plain words, a one-minute **Start here** tour, **Export** to send a copy to anyone as one HTML file, a layout for **phones and tablets** with drag and pinch, search, keyboard shortcuts, and right-click actions on every card. ### Also: blueprints, for apps you haven't built yet Floorplan is made for mapping code you already have. It can also start from a PRD, a spec or a description of something you want to build, and draw a **blueprint**: the same kind of map, showing every part, file, endpoint and screen you'd need and how they'd fit together. Cards are dashed to show it's a plan. Instead of a Health check you get a review of what the plan still leaves open, each part ## See it in action Want to click around yourself? Open the [live demo](https://haydenschmitty.github.io/floorplan-demo/): the real Brewline map beside a scripted conversation, in Claude Code or Codex.

Ask the map. A real answer, from the Claude Code CLI in 31 seconds. It traced the gift from form to inbox across two repos, and spotted two bugs along the way.

Start from a screen. Pick any page and see everything behind it, from the button down to the database and outside services.

Recent work. What you asked for, what changed, and why each change was needed, on one board.

Health check. A password left in the code and an endpoint anyone can call, each with a one-click fix prompt.

Zoom in. Inside any part: what's in it, what uses it, and what it relies on. Green tags mark what just changed.

Guided flows. Watch a request travel through the app step by step, or ask for a new one to be traced.
## Install You need [Node.js 18+](https://nodejs.org) and either Claude Code or Codex. Floorplan runs on the plan you already have, with no API keys. ### Claude Code In the desktop app's Code tab or the CLI: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan claude plugin install floorplan@floorplan ``` Start a new session and it's ready. Installing the Claude Code CLI is recommended even if you use the desktop app, because it lets the map's Ask bar read your real code. More in [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md). ### Codex Signed in with ChatGPT. No terminal needed: 1. In the Codex app, open **Plugins** and choose **Add a marketplace**. 2. For **Source**, enter `haydenschmitty/floorplan` and click **Add marketplace**. 3. Find **Floorplan** and click **+** to install it. Or, from a terminal: ```bash codex plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan codex plugin add floorplan@floorplan ``` Start a new chat and ask for a floorplan, or type `$floorplan`. The map's Ask bar runs on your own Codex sign-in, with no API key. More in [Floorplan in Codex](docs/codex.md). ## Quick start 1. Open your project in Claude Code or Codex. For a frontend and backend in separate repos, open the folder that holds both. 2. Ask: > Make me a floorplan of this app. (In Codex you can also type `$floorplan`.) 3. Explore. The map opens on its own, starting with a short tour. When you've done more work, ask: > Update the floorplan. Only what changed is re-read, and what you just worked on lights up under **Recent work**. **No code yet?** Floorplan can plan an app from a PRD or spec instead. Share the document and ask: > Here's my PRD. Make me a floorplan of what we'd need to build. You get a [blueprint](#also-blueprints-for-apps-you-havent-built-yet) of the planned system, clearly marked as a plan. ### Things to try | Ask Claude Code or Codex | Ask the map | |---|---| | "Make me a floorplan of this app" | "What happens when someone places an order?" | | "Update the floorplan" | "Where do we talk to Stripe?" | | "Fix the important issues from the floorplan's Health check" | "If I change the users table, what breaks?" | | "Add a flow showing how a new user signs up" | "Which files handle login?" | | "Rewrite the floorplan for developers" | "What did we change for refunds?" | | "Export the floorplan so I can send it to the team" | | ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart LR code["Your codebase
one repo or several"] --> scan["Scan
files, imports, routes, requests"] scan --> agent["Claude or Codex
names the parts, describes every file"] agent --> build["Build
map, health, screens, recent work"] build --> map["floorplan/index.html
opens in your browser"] map -. "update the floorplan" .-> scan ``` Scripts do the mechanical work: finding repos, parsing code in a dozen languages, matching web requests to endpoints, laying out the map. They're plain Node with no dependencies. Claude or Codex does the part only a reader can: deciding what the parts of your app *are*, and saying so plainly. Details in [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md). **Languages:** TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Scala, plus Vue, Svelte and Astro files, with lighter support for others.
**Endpoints:** Express, Koa, Hono, Next.js, Firebase Cloud Functions, Flask, FastAPI, Django, Go's net/http, Gin, Echo and chi, Actix, Axum, Spring.
**Screens:** Next.js, React Router, Vue, SvelteKit, Remix, Nuxt, Astro, Expo, Angular, TanStack. ## What it adds to your project A `floorplan/` folder holding the map. In Claude Code, if you say yes, it also adds a short section to `CLAUDE.local.md` so future sessions know the map is there. **Neither is committed:** the folder ignores itself in git, and `CLAUDE.local.md` goes in your clone's private ignore list. In Codex, only the `floorplan/` folder is added. Your `.gitignore` and other tracked files are never touched. See ## Privacy - The scan, the map and its small local server all run on your computer. The server only accepts connections from your own machine. - No dependencies or install scripts, and the map works offline: its layout engine and fonts are built in. - Questions on the map go to your own account, through the Claude Code CLI or Codex, which can read your code but not change it. - The Health check never stores or shows secret values, only where they are. - No analytics or tracking. The map may ask once whether you'd like an email when Floorplan Cloud launches. Nothing is sent unless you sign up, and then only your email and "just me" or "with my team". More in [Privacy and security](docs/privacy-and-security.md). Wondering whether a plugin is safe to install? [Is it safe to install?](docs/is-it-safe.md) lists everything Floorplan does on your computer, how a test checks that on every change, and how to verify your copy. ## Documentation | | | |---|---| | [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | Install, first map, updating, planning from a PRD, removing | | [Floorplan in Codex](docs/codex.md) | Installing and using it in Codex | | [Using the map](docs/using-the-map.md) | Every button, view, shortcut and menu | | [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md) | The pipeline, connection matching, refreshes | | [What's in your project](docs/project-files.md) | Every file Floorplan creates, and how to edit it | | [Privacy and security](docs/privacy-and-security.md) | What runs where, and what leaves your machine | | [Is it safe to install?](docs/is-it-safe.md) | No hooks, MCP servers, dependencies or downloads; every program it runs; checking your installed copy | | [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Common problems and fixes | | [Developing Floorplan](docs/development.md) | Repo layout, local installs, releases | ## FAQ
Is it safe to install? Floorplan has no hooks, no MCP servers and no dependencies, downloads nothing, and never runs code from the internet. Its only outside request is the opt-in waitlist. A test checks all of that on every change, and every release lists a fingerprint of each file so you can confirm your installed copy is the real thing. Everything is in [Is it safe to install?](docs/is-it-safe.md).
Does my code leave my computer? Only the way Claude Code and Codex always work: the AI reads the files it needs to describe your app, through your own account. The map itself is a local file and its server only listens on your machine. If you choose to open the map in the Claude app instead, Claude uploads the map (names, descriptions and structure, not your source code) to your private claude.ai account, and asks first. The one
How long does it take, and what does it cost? A first map takes a few minutes for a small app and longer for a big one, because every file and endpoint gets described. It uses your Claude or ChatGPT plan like any other task. Big projects are split across parallel helpers. Updates re-read only what changed, so they're quick and cheap.
Do I need a CLI for the Ask bar? No. The map works without one. The Ask bar answers through the Claude Code CLI or Codex, which can read your real code. Codex's desktop app already includes what it needs. With Claude, without the CLI you can ask from the Claude app instead, using the map alone.
Will it change or commit my files? It only writes its own `floorplan/` folder (and, in Claude Code if you say yes, a section in `CLAUDE.local.md`), and neither is committed. It never changes your code, your `.gitignore` or your `CLAUDE.md`.
The names it picked aren't how we talk about it. Can I change them? Yes. Just ask ("rename 'Main server' to 'Shop API' on the floorplan"), or edit `floorplan/architecture.json` and `floorplan/descriptions/` yourself. Your edits are kept on every update.
Does it work with Codex as well as Claude Code? Yes. It's the same plugin, the same map and the same Health check. Each app runs it on your own plan: Claude Code on your Claude account, Codex on your ChatGPT sign-in. A map made in one opens fine with the other. See [Floorplan in Codex](docs/codex.md).
Can I use it before I've written any code? Yes, though mapping existing code is what it's mainly for. Share a PRD, a spec or a description of your app and ask for a floorplan, and you get a blueprint: a map of what you'd need to build, marked as a plan, with a review of the decisions still open. You can change it from the map, then switch to a map of the real code once it's built. See [Plan something you haven't built yet](docs/getting-sta
Does it work on monorepos and multi-repo setups? Yes. Point it at a monorepo, a subfolder of one, or a plain folder that holds several repos side by side. It finds every repo and connects them.
How is this different from Archify or Understand Anything? Archify draws diagrams of anything, and Understand Anything builds a developer's knowledge graph of a codebase. Floorplan maps the app you built, in plain English, and tells you what's risky and what your AI just changed. See [Floorplan, Archify or Understand Anything?](#floorplan-archify-or-understand-anything)
## Contributing Issues and pull requests are welcome. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Developing Floorplan](docs/development.md). ## License [MIT](LICENSE) © 2026 [Hayden Smith](https://github.com/haydenschmitty) Shell cwd was reset to /Users/hosanglee/archy

Start with the whole app, then double-click into a part, a group of files, a file, and its endpoints. Each view shows what it's used by and what it uses. 		**💬 Plain English everywhere**

# How it works Floorplan splits the work between scripts and the AI you run it in, Claude Code or Codex. The scripts do everything mechanical: finding files, parsing code, matching requests to endpoints, laying out the map. They're plain Node.js with no dependencies, and they cost no tokens. The AI does what only a reader of the code can: deciding what the parts of your app *are*, and explaining them plainly. ```mermaid flowchart TD status["status: is there a map already?"] -->|no| scan status -->|yes| refresh["refresh: re-scan, carry over what didn't change"] scan["scan: repos, files, imports, endpoints, requests"] --> arch["The AI writes architecture.json
the parts of the app, outside services, flows, tour"] arch --> build["build: assign files, connect everything,
Health, screens, the map"] build --> describe["The AI names and describes every file and endpoint"] describe --> recent["The AI marks recent work"] refresh --> describe recent --> open["open: serve the map and show it"] ``` ## 1. Scan `scan.mjs` finds every git repository under the folder you point it at (one repo, a monorepo, or several repos side by side), skipping duplicate worktrees. It lists files with git, so your `.gitignore` is respected, then extracts from each file: - **imports**, resolved to real files: TypeScript path aliases, Python packages, Go modules, Rust crates, JVM packages; - **exported definitions** and their doc comments; - **endpoints** the server defines; - **web requests** the code makes; - content **fingerprints**, so later updates can tell what changed. Supported languages: TypeScript and JavaScript (including Vue, Svelte and Astro files), Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Scala and Groovy, with lighter support for others. ## 2. Connecting requests to endpoints The most useful lines on the map connect a screen's web requests to the server code that answers them, often across repos. Floorplan: - **Finds endpoints** in Express, Koa, Hono, Next.js (route files and API routes), Firebase Cloud Functions, Flask, FastAPI, Django, Go (net/http, Gin, Echo, chi, Fiber), Actix, Axum and Spring. - **Resolves prefixes**: Flask blueprints registered with a `url_prefix`, and Express routers mounted with `app.use('/api/users', usersRouter)`, including routers mounted inside other routers and mounts with middleware in front. - **Finds requests** made with `fetch`, axios, ky, `requests` and similar, including: - addresses built in a variable first: `const url = …; api.get(url)`; - template strings with nested parts; - small helpers in the same file that add a prefix, like `call('/definitions')`. - **Firebase Cloud Functions** are called by name rather than by address. A callable function (`onCall`) shows up as `CALL /approveItem` under the name your functions entry file exports it as, and the website's `httpsCallable(functions, 'approveItem')` calls reach it, including through a helper of your own that wraps `httpsCallable`. An `onRequest` function is an ordinary endpoint at `/`, and an Express app passed to it keeps its own routes under that name. Scheduled and other background f - **Matches** the two. When a request only spells out part of the address, because the base URL lives in settings, Floorplan learns each client's base path and prefers matches that fit it. It's pattern matching, not a compiler, so it catches most connections but not all. If an important link is missing, ask for it to be added to the floorplan, and it will record it as an explicit connection. ## 3. The AI describes the system Claude or Codex reads the scan summary, READMEs, setup files and entry points, then writes `architecture.json`: - the main parts of your app, each with a plain summary; - the outside services it really talks to (databases, payment providers, email); - connections the scan can't see, like queues, scheduled jobs and webhooks; - a few guided flows and a "Start here" tour. The build then assigns every file to the deepest part whose patterns match, and reports anything left over. Next, `describe.mjs` writes a worksheet for each part. A worksheet is a digest of every file and endpoint: what it defines, its doc comments, what it uses and what uses it. The AI fills in a name and description for each. On large projects, Claude Code splits the worksheets across parallel helpers. By default everything is written for the app's owner, not an engineer: what each thing does for the business, in everyday words. Ask for a developer-facing map and it switches to technical style. ## 4. Build `build.mjs` validates everything the AI wrote and reports problems by name ("did you mean …"). It then: - connects the parts, using imports, matched requests and the AI's explicit connections; - runs the **Health** check; - detects **screens**: Next.js, React Router, Vue, SvelteKit, Remix, Nuxt, Astro, Expo, Angular, TanStack; - writes `graph.json` and the self-contained `index.html`, noting whether Claude Code or Codex made it, so the map's Ask bar and fix prompts name the right one. The map lays itself out in your browser with [ELK](https://eclipse.dev/elk/), so the build itself is fast. ## 5. Recent work After every make or update, the AI records what was just worked on in `recent-work.json`. `recent.mjs` lists the facts: what changed since the last map, uncommitted changes, and recent commits, each matched to its card. The AI adds the *why*: what you asked for, and how each change serves it. The previous highlights are replaced every time. ## 6. Showing it `open.mjs` starts the map's small local server in the background and opens your browser. If the server is already running for this map, it's reused, and any open tab reloads itself in place instead of a new one opening. ## Updates `refresh.mjs` re-scans and compares against the last build, using each file's fingerprint: - **exact content**, which spots edits, renames and moves; - **signature**: its exports, endpoints and doc comments. Edits inside function bodies don't count. It then: - carries descriptions over to moved and renamed files and endpoints; - drops entries for deleted files; - flags entries whose signature changed, for review. Then it rebuilds. The AI only has to describe what's new or flagged, and check the structure if the change was large. That's why updates are quick. ## Blueprints Everything above is how Floorplan maps existing code, its main job. A blueprint is the other way in: a map of something that isn't built yet. The AI reads a PRD or a description and writes `floorplan/plan.json`: every file and endpoint the system would need, which screen calls which endpoint, which parts use outside services and the database, and who may use each endpoint. It also lists the stack it chose, its assumptions and the questions the PRD leaves open. `plan.mjs` turns the plan into the same scan `scan.mjs` makes from code, so the build, Screens, flows, the tour and Ask all work the same way. The differences: - cards have dashed outlines and the board a **Blueprint** label; - Health becomes a **design review** of the plan: endpoints anyone could use to change data, endpoints with no decision on who may use them, open questions, and pieces nothing connects to; - every part has **Build this with Claude** (or Codex): a request to build that part as planned, listing its files, endpoints and what it relies on; - Ask answers from the plan and the PRD, since there's no code to read; - the Ask bar's **Change** switch takes requests like "also plan out refunds": the agent returns the updated plan, the map's server checks it with `plan.mjs` and `build.mjs` (sending problems back once), saves it and redraws the map with the changes highlighted, and **Undo** puts the previous plan back. Each design review item's **Resolve on the map** fills in that request for you: an open question just needs your answer. The agent stays read-only: only the server writes, and only `plan.json`, ` Updating a blueprint redraws it from `plan.json`. Once the code exists, `refresh.mjs --from-code` maps the real code instead, and `plan.json` stays. ## Asking questions The map's server answers each question with the AI on your computer, in your project: - **Claude Code:** it runs `claude -p` with read-only tools only: reading and searching files, and `floorplan/query.mjs`, which looks things up in the map. - **Codex:** it runs `codex exec` in Codex's read-only sandbox, with the same lookups. These runs aren't saved to your Codex history, so a follow-up brings the last few questions and answers along. It uses whichever made the map, and the other one if that isn't installed. Either way it answers with text plus the cards to show, so answers can cite real code. In the Claude app, the map asks Claude through the app instead, with the same lookups but no access to your source. The same lookups help ordinary Claude Code sessions. If you say yes after your first map, the short section Floorplan adds to `CLAUDE.local.md` tells them to check the map (`query.mjs find`, `show`, `path`, `overview`) before searching the code from scratch. # architecture.json schema

`floorplan/architecture.json` describes the structure: subsystems, modules, external services, flows. Names and descriptions for individual files and routes go in `floorplan/descriptions/*.json` instead (see [writing-descriptions.md](writing-descriptions.md)). They're kept separate so parallel agents can write them without conflicts. `build.mjs` checks both against the scan and reports problems by

Contents: [Top level](#top-level) · [nodes](#nodes) · [Assignment rules](#how-files-get-assigned) · [edges](#edges) · [annotations](#annotations) · [flows](#flows) · [Recent work](#recent-work) · [Full example](#full-example)

## Top level

| field | type | required | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `$schema` | `"floorplan/architecture@1"` | no | marker |
| `project` | object | yes | `name` (string, required), `summary` (1–3 sentences), `entrypoints` (file paths) |
| `nodes` | array | yes | subsystems and modules. See below |
| `edges` | array | no | connections the scanner can't see |
| `annotations` | array | no | notes pinned to specific files |
| `flows` | array | no | guided walkthroughs through the board |
| `tour` | array | no | the "Start here" tour shown on first open: 3–8 stops `{ "node": "<node id or file path>", "title": "…", "note": "…" }`, in plain language, in the order a newcomer should see them. The first flow is appended automatically |
| `audience` | `"everyone"` \| `"developers"` | no | who names and descriptions are written for. Default `"everyone"`: plain language a non-technical owner understands (what it does for the business, in everyday words). `"developers"`: technical style for engineers |
| `include` | string[] | no | file categories to map. Default `["code"]`. Others: `config`, `docs` |
| `ignore` | string[] | no | globs for files to leave off the board entirely (generated code, vendored libs, fixtures) |

## nodes

Each node is a chip on the board. Hierarchy comes from `parent`. A node with no parent sits on the top-level board.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | unique; letters, digits, `_ - .`. Convention: dotted by parent (`api.orders`) |
| `label` | string | short display name ("Orders API") |
| `kind` | enum | `ui` `service` `worker` `library` `feature` `data` `config` `test` `script` `infra` `external` |
| `parent` | string | id of the enclosing node |
| `summary` | string | one sentence: what it's responsible for |
| `details` | string | optional longer notes; blank lines separate paragraphs |
| `paths` | string[] | globs claiming files (see below) |
| `exclude` | string[] | globs to carve files back out of `paths`. **Inherited by all descendants**, e.g. `"exclude": ["**/*.test.tsx"]` on a frontend node keeps co-located tests out of every child, so a separate Tests node can claim them |
| `packages` | string[] | **external nodes:** package names this node stands for, e.g. `"stripe"`, `"npm:@stripe/*"`, `"pypi:sqlalchemy"`. Imports of them become edges to this node |
| `hosts` | string[] | **external nodes:** hostnames called from code, e.g. `"api.stripe.com"`, `"*.squareup.com"`. Calls become `http` edges |
| `tags` | string[] | free-form, shown in the panel |

Kinds, briefly:
- `ui`: frontends and apps
- `service`: a deployable server
- `worker`: background jobs and queues
- `library`: shared code
- `feature`: a vertical slice inside a service or UI
- `data`: models, migrations, the DB layer
- `config`
- `test`
- `script`: one-off and ops scripts
- `infra`: deploy, CI, IaC
- `external`: databases and third-party APIs. These own no files.

### Glob syntax
- `**` matches any number of directories, `*` stays within one path segment, `?` matches one character, `{a,b}` is alternation.
- A whole folder name in brackets, like `[id]`, `[...slug]` or `[[...slug]]` (Next.js, SvelteKit), matches that folder literally: `app/orders/[id]/**`. Elsewhere, `[abc]` matches one of those characters.
- A pattern with no wildcard also matches as a directory: `backend/app` equals `backend/app/**`.
- Paths are relative to the codebase root. In a multi-repo root they start with the repo folder.

### How files get assigned
Every included file goes to exactly one node:
1. Collect the nodes whose `paths` match the file and whose `exclude` doesn't.
2. The **deepest** node wins, so a child beats its parent. You can give a parent a broad glob (`web/**`) and children narrower ones; files no child claims stay on the parent.
3. Between nodes at the same depth, the glob with the longer literal prefix wins. Real ties are warned about.
4. Files no node claims go to an automatic **Unassigned** chip. Keep it under ~10%.

In the viewer, a node with more than ~24 files of its own groups them into folder chips automatically, so you don't need a node for every directory. Make a node when it means something.

## edges

Only add what static analysis can't find. Imports (`import`) and HTTP calls matched to routes (`http`) are already in the scan.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `from`, `to` | string | node id **or** file path |
| `kind` | enum | `import` `call` `http` `rpc` `event` `queue` `data` `config` |
| `label` | string | short, e.g. `"POST /orders"`, `"order.paid"`, `"reads/writes"` |
| `description` | string | optional sentence shown when the trace is clicked |

Good candidates:
- service → database (`data`)
- publisher → queue → consumer (`queue` / `event`)
- webhooks coming in from third parties (`http`, from the external node to the handler)
- cron/scheduler → job (`call`)
- Firebase background functions (schedules, Firestore/Storage/Pub/Sub triggers, from the scan's FIREBASE FUNCTIONS list) → a `worker` node; link the collection or topic that triggers them (`event`)
- calls through env-configured base URLs that the matcher missed (`http`)

## annotations

`{ "path": "<file>", "note": "…", "tags": ["hotspot"] }` pins a note to a file. The file's chip gets an accent outline. Use these sparingly, for god-files, tricky invariants, or deprecated code still in use.

## flows

```json
{ "id": "checkout", "title": "Checkout", "description": "optional",
  "steps": [ { "node": "web.cart", "note": "User clicks Pay" }, { "node": "api.orders", "note": "Creates the order" } ] }
```
- Each step's `node` is a node id or a file path. There must be at least 2 steps.
- The viewer moves to the board where each pair of consecutive steps is visible and animates a signal between them.
- Write the notes as a narration a new engineer would want.

## recent work

`floorplan/recent-work.json` is a separate file, rewritten on every make and update. It holds what was just worked on, framed against what the user asked for. The viewer gives those cards a green "Changed"/"New" tag, shows "N changed" on the parts containing them, adds each `note` to the card's hover, and lists the tasks under a **Recent work** button and in the overview panel.

```json
{
  "updatedAt": "2026-10-27T10:30:00Z",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "title": "Refunds from the order page",
      "request": "Let staff refund an order straight from its order page",
      "summary": "Staff can now refund all or part of an order from its page. The money goes back to the customer's card through Stripe, and they get an email. Refunds over $500 need a manager.",
      "items": [
        { "ref": "shop-api/app/services/refunds.py", "change": "new", "note": "New: works out how much to refund, sends it back through Stripe and records it on the order. This is the heart of what was asked." },
        { "ref": "POST /api/orders/<int:order_id>/refund", "change": "new", "note": "The request the Refund button sends; it checks the manager limit before anything is refunded." }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

# How it works Floorplan splits the work between scripts and the AI you run it in, Claude Code or Codex. The scripts do everything mechanical: finding files, parsing code, matching requests to endpoints, laying out the map. They're plain Node.js with no dependencies, and they cost no tokens. The AI does what only a reader of the code can: deciding what the parts of your app *are*, and explaining them plainly. ```mermaid flowchart TD status["status: is there a map already?"] -->|no| scan status -->|yes| refresh["refresh: re-scan, carry over what didn't change"] scan["scan: repos, files, imports, endpoints, requests"] --> arch["The AI writes architecture.json
the parts of the app, outside services, flows, tour"] arch --> build["build: assign files, connect everything,
Health, screens, the map"] build --> describe["The AI names and describes every file and endpoint"] describe --> recent["The AI marks recent work"] refresh --> describe recent --> open["open: serve the map and show it"] ``` ## 1. Scan `scan.mjs` finds every git repository under the folder you point it at (one repo, a monorepo, or several repos side by side), skipping duplicate worktrees. It lists files with git, so your `.gitignore` is respected, then extracts from each file: - **imports**, resolved to real files: TypeScript path aliases, Python packages, Go modules, Rust crates, JVM packages; - **exported definitions** and their doc comments; - **endpoints** the server defines; - **web requests** the code makes; - content **fingerprints**, so later updates can tell what changed. Supported languages: TypeScript and JavaScript (including Vue, Svelte and Astro files), Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Scala and Groovy, with lighter support for others. ## 2. Connecting requests to endpoints The most useful lines on the map connect a screen's web requests to the server code that answers them, often across repos. Floorplan: - **Finds endpoints** in Express, Koa, Hono, Next.js (route files and API routes), Firebase Cloud Functions, Flask, FastAPI, Django, Go (net/http, Gin, Echo, chi, Fiber), Actix, Axum and Spring. - **Resolves prefixes**: Flask blueprints registered with a `url_prefix`, and Express routers mounted with `app.use('/api/users', usersRouter)`, including routers mounted inside other routers and mounts with middleware in front. - **Finds requests** made with `fetch`, axios, ky, `requests` and similar, including: - addresses built in a variable first: `const url = …; api.get(url)`; - template strings with nested parts; - small helpers in the same file that add a prefix, like `call('/definitions')`. - **Firebase Cloud Functions** are called by name rather than by address. A callable function (`onCall`) shows up as `CALL /approveItem` under the name your functions entry file exports it as, and the website's `httpsCallable(functions, 'approveItem')` calls reach it, including through a helper of your own that wraps `httpsCallable`. An `onRequest` function is an ordinary endpoint at `/`, and an Express app passed to it keeps its own routes under that name. Scheduled and other background f - **Matches** the two. When a request only spells out part of the address, because the base URL lives in settings, Floorplan learns each client's base path and prefers matches that fit it. It's pattern matching, not a compiler, so it catches most connections but not all. If an important link is missing, ask for it to be added to the floorplan, and it will record it as an explicit connection. ## 3. The AI describes the system Claude or Codex reads the scan summary, READMEs, setup files and entry points, then writes `architecture.json`: - the main parts of your app, each with a plain summary; - the outside services it really talks to (databases, payment providers, email); - connections the scan can't see, like queues, scheduled jobs and webhooks; - a few guided flows and a "Start here" tour. The build then assigns every file to the deepest part whose patterns match, and reports anything left over. Next, `describe.mjs` writes a worksheet for each part. A worksheet is a digest of every file and endpoint: what it defines, its doc comments, what it uses and what uses it. The AI fills in a name and description for each. On large projects, Claude Code splits the worksheets across parallel helpers. By default everything is written for the app's owner, not an engineer: what each thing does for the business, in everyday words. Ask for a developer-facing map and it switches to technical style. ## 4. Build `build.mjs` validates everything the AI wrote and reports problems by name ("did you mean …"). It then: - connects the parts, using imports, matched requests and the AI's explicit connections; - runs the **Health** check; - detects **screens**: Next.js, React Router, Vue, SvelteKit, Remix, Nuxt, Astro, Expo, Angular, TanStack; - writes `graph.json` and the self-contained `index.html`, noting whether Claude Code or Codex made it, so the map's Ask bar and fix prompts name the right one. The map lays itself out in your browser with [ELK](https://eclipse.dev/elk/), so the build itself is fast. ## 5. Recent work After every make or update, the AI records what was just worked on in `recent-work.json`. `recent.mjs` lists the facts: what changed since the last map, uncommitted changes, and recent commits, each matched to its card. The AI adds the *why*: what you asked for, and how each change serves it. The previous highlights are replaced every time. ## 6. Showing it `open.mjs` starts the map's small local server in the background and opens your browser. If the server is already running for this map, it's reused, and any open tab reloads itself in place instead of a new one opening. ## Updates `refresh.mjs` re-scans and compares against the last build, using each file's fingerprint: - **exact content**, which spots edits, renames and moves; - **signature**: its exports, endpoints and doc comments. Edits inside function bodies don't count. The AI only has to describe what's new or flagged, and check the structure if the change was large. | `audience` | `"everyone"` \| `"developers"` | no | who names and descriptions are written for. Default `"everyone"`: plain language a non-technical owner understands (what it does for the business, in everyday words). `"developers"`: technical style for engineers |
| `include` | string[] | no | file categories to map. Default `["code"]`. Others: `config`, `docs` |
| `ignore` | string[] | no | globs for files to leave off the board entirely (generated code, vendored libs, fixtures) |

## nodes

Each node is a chip on the board. Hierarchy comes from `parent`. A node with no parent sits on the top-level board.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | unique; letters, digits, `_ - .`. Convention: dotted by parent (`api.orders`) |
| `label` | string | short display name ("Orders API") |
| `kind` | enum | `ui` `service` `worker` `library` `feature` `data` `config` `test` `script` `infra` `external` |
| `parent` | string | id of the enclosing node |
| `summary` | string | one sentence: what it's responsible for |
| `details` | string | optional longer notes; blank lines separate paragraphs |
| `paths` | string[] | globs claiming files (see below) |
| `exclude` | string[] | globs to carve files back out of `paths`. **Inherited by all descendants**, e.g. `"exclude": ["**/*.test.tsx"]` on a frontend node keeps co-located tests out of every child, so a separate Tests node can claim them |
| `packages` | string[] | **external nodes:** package names this node stands for, e.g. `"stripe"`, `"npm:@stripe/*"`, `"pypi:sqlalchemy"`. Imports of them become edges to this node |
| `hosts` | string[] | **external nodes:** hostnames called from code, e.g. `"api.stripe.com"`, `"*.squareup.com"`. Calls become `http` edges |
| `tags` | string[] | free-form, shown in the panel |

Kinds, briefly:
- `ui`: frontends and apps
- `service`: a deployable server
- `worker`: background jobs and queues
- `library`: shared code
- `feature`: a vertical slice inside a service or UI
- `data`: models, migrations, the DB layer
- `config`
- `test`
- `script`: one-off and ops scripts
- `infra`: deploy, CI, IaC
- `external`: databases and third-party APIs. These own no files.

### Glob syntax
- `**` matches any number of directories, `*` stays within one path segment, `?` matches one character, `{a,b}` is alternation.
- A whole folder name in brackets, like `[id]`, `[...slug]` or `[[...slug]]` (Next.js, SvelteKit), matches that folder literally: `app/orders/[id]/**`. Elsewhere, `[abc]` matches one of those characters.
- A pattern with no wildcard also matches as a directory: `backend/app` equals `backend/app/**`.
- Paths are relative to the codebase root. In a multi-repo root they start with the repo folder.

### How files get assigned
Every included file goes to exactly one node:
1. Collect the nodes whose `paths` match the file and whose `exclude` doesn't.
2. The **deepest** node wins, so a child beats its parent. You can give a parent a broad glob (`web/**`) and children narrower ones; files no child claims stay on the parent.
3. Between nodes at the same depth, the glob with the longer literal prefix wins. Real ties are warned about.
4. Files no node claims go to an automatic **Unassigned** chip. Keep it under ~10%.

In the viewer, a node with more than ~24 files of its own groups them into folder chips automatically, so you don't need a node for every directory. Make a node when it means something.

## edges

Only add what static analysis can't find. Imports (`import`) and HTTP calls matched to routes (`http`) are already in the scan.

| field | type | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `from`, `to` | string | node id **or** file path |
| `kind` | enum | `import` `call` `http` `rpc` `event` `queue` `data` `config` |
| `label` | string | short, e.g. `"POST /orders"`, `"order.paid"`, `"reads/writes"` |
| `description` | string | optional sentence shown when the trace is clicked |

Good candidates:
- service → database (`data`)
- publisher → queue → consumer (`queue` / `event`)
- webhooks coming in from third parties (`http`, from the external node to the handler)
- cron/scheduler → job (`call`)
- Firebase background functions (schedules, Firestore/Storage/Pub/Sub triggers, from the scan's FIREBASE FUNCTIONS list) → a `worker` node; link the collection or topic that triggers them (`event`)
- calls through env-configured base URLs that the matcher missed (`http`)

## annotations

`{ "path": "<file>", "note": "…", "tags": ["hotspot"] }` pins a note to a file. The file's chip gets an accent outline. Use these sparingly, for god-files, tricky invariants, or deprecated code still in use.

## flows

```json
{ "id": "checkout", "title": "Checkout", "description": "optional",
  "steps": [ { "node": "web.cart", "note": "User clicks Pay" }, { "node": "api.orders", "note": "Creates the order" } ] }
```
- Each step's `node` is a node id or a file path. There must be at least 2 steps.
- The viewer moves to the board where each pair of consecutive steps is visible and animates a signal between them.
- Write the notes as a narration a new engineer would want.

## recent work

`floorplan/recent-work.json` is a separate file, rewritten on every make and update. It holds what was just worked on, framed against what the user asked for. The viewer gives those cards a green "Changed"/"New" tag, shows "N changed" on the parts containing them, adds each `note` to the card's hover, and lists the tasks under a **Recent work** button and in the overview panel.

```json
{
  "updatedAt": "2026-10-27T10:30:00Z",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "title": "Refunds from the order page",
      "request": "Let staff refund an order straight from its order page",
      "summary": "Staff can now refund all or part of an order from its page. The money goes back to the customer's card through Stripe, and they get an email. Refunds over $500 need a manager.",
      "items": [
        { "ref": "shop-api/app/services/refunds.py", "change": "new", "note": "New: works out how much to refund, sends it back through Stripe and records it on the order. This is the heart of what was asked." },
        { "ref": "POST /api/orders/<int:order_id>/refund", "change": "new", "note": "The request the Refund button sends; it checks the manager limit before anything is refunded." }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

# Spec: visualization surface (static export + terminal-native live)

Status: Branch A shipped in scoped form (`dsm` + `trend`); Branch B still
design. Tracking: [#283]; branches
[#284] (static export, first) and [#285] (terminal-native live). This spec fixes the scope, the
anti-theater gate, and the two-branch plan before any UI code lands. It is the
first archy feature whose primary user is the **human governor**, not the
agent, so the framing guardrails matter more than usual.

## 1. The gap

archy computes every structural signal worth showing and renders **none** of
it. `archy graph --format dot` emits Graphviz DOT (`cli.py`) that nothing draws;
`.archy/history.jsonl` is a per-commit time series of the five axes that nothing
plots; `watcher.py` already runs a `watchdog` observer (2s debounce) inside
`archy mcp`, so the live event stream a real-time view needs already exists.

sentrux (MIT, pure-Rust desktop GUI + hosted scanner, 52 languages) fills this
with a live interactive treemap whose files glow as the agent edits them. Their
own pitch is explicitly human-facing: the terminal took away the IDE file-tree,
so you can no longer see a cycle form or an internal module leak as it happens.

**Positioning, stated honestly.** archy's core loop is agent-first: the agent
reads JSON and self-corrects on the score. Visualization does not improve that
loop; it serves a *different* user, the human watching the agent. We are not
out-treemapping a funded Rust desktop app on breadth (52 languages, native GUI).
We win by being the free, MIT, **terminal-native**, Python/agent-first tool that
*also* renders, staying where the agent session already runs.

## 2. Anti-theater gate (normative)

A generic force-directed import graph does **not** ship as a headline. It is
pretty, low-signal, present in every tool, and already conveyed to the agent as
JSON. A visual earns a slot only when it makes a signal archy *uniquely*
computes faster to grok than text. Exactly four qualify, and every view must
encode at least one:

1. **edit-risk heatmap** - nodes colored by `edit_risk`; the hot nodes are where
   the next agent edit is dangerous.
2. **cycle tangles** - SCC membership highlighted (the acyclicity axis; near
----
1:# Axis review: are the 5 axes sufficient? Should `calls_per_edge` become the 6th?
8:- **`calls_per_edge` should not be promoted to a 6th axis.** It passes the orthogonality check but fails the directionality, actionability, and discriminant-validity checks an OECD-style composite indicator requires.
9:- The best candidate if a 6th axis is ever added was **type-hint coverage** (Python-specific, clear direction, cheap to compute, actionable). **Empirics ran in 2026-05** and concluded against shipping it in any form: independence is the weakest archy has measured (max `|r| = 0.551`), discriminant validity is contested (django / numpy / boto3 at near-zero coverage are widely-respected codebases), and the value-prop argument against even a diagnostic surface is strong (better tools own the niche, the signal is not structural, and the slippery slope toward "complete-codebase-health sensor" dilutes archy's graph-shape focus). See [`TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md`](TYPE_HINT_COVERAGE_EMPIRICS.md). No 6th-axis candidate is currently active.
10:- The right home for call-graph data is **a refinement of the existing modularity axis** (call-weighted Newman Q) and **agent-navigation MCP tools** (already shipped). Neither requires a new axis.
16:The v0.16 introduction of `calls_per_edge` as a diagnostic, and the strong orthogonality numbers it produced on the 27-project benchmark, set up an implicit expectation that it would be promoted to a score axis "at a deliberate version boundary." After `complexity` shipped in v0.20, `calls_per_edge` is the natural next candidate. This document asks whether it should be.
25:## What each existing axis catches, and what it doesn't
27:| axis | catches | misses |
35:As a 5-axis system this covers:
54:**Orthogonality.** Max `|r| = 0.229` against modularity, acyclicity, depth, equality, propagation_cost. Below the OECD redundancy threshold (`|r| > 0.7`) by a wide margin. More orthogonal than the typical existing inter-axis pair: on the current bench the 10 inter-axis pairs have **median `|r| = 0.32`, max `0.61`** (modularity ↔ depth); `calls_per_edge`'s 0.229 sits below even the median pair. (An earlier draft cited "median ~0.45"; that figure was not reproducible against the committed correlation matrix in [`bench/results.md`](../../bench/results.md) and has been corrected.)
64:This is the case [`RESEARCH_METRICS.md` section 16](RESEARCH_METRICS.md) makes. The orthogonality numbers are real. They are also **necessary but not sufficient** for adding the axis to the score.
83:The signal is correlated with **codebase shape**, not **codebase health**. The strongest direct evidence is that `calls_per_edge` barely correlates with archy's own composite at all: across the 28-project bench, **Pearson `r = -0.03`, Spearman `+0.18`** between `calls_per_edge` and `overall`. A would-be quality axis that is statistically uncorrelated with the quality composite is, almost by definition, not measuring the same thing. Mechanistically:
113:If ten experienced Python architects ranked the 27 bench projects on architectural quality and we computed the Spearman correlation of that ranking with each archy axis, would `calls_per_edge` rank well or poorly?
----
Usage: archy graph [OPTIONS] [PATH]

  Build the import graph for a Python project rooted at PATH.

Options:
  --format [json|dot|text]  Output format.
  --internal-only           Hide edges to external (third-party / stdlib)
                            modules.
  --help                    Show this message and exit.
Usage: archy render [OPTIONS] [PATH]

  Render a view as a self-contained HTML file (offline, no JS, no CDN).

  `--view=dsm` draws the Design Structure Matrix, back-edges in red;
  `--view=trend` plots the five axes over .archy/history.jsonl. Output is
  byte-stable for a fixed input, so two exports diff cleanly.

  Options are per-view (see the `dsm view:` / `trend view:` help text) and
  ignored by the other view. There is no `graph` view: a node-link diagram
  needs a vendored layout engine and carries the least signal of the three, so
  it stays deferred (docs/SPEC_VISUALIZATION.md).

Options:
  --view [dsm|trend]              Which view to render.  [default: dsm]
  --out FILE                      Write the HTML here. Defaults to stdout.
  --group [community|layer|topological]
                                  dsm view: how to order rows/columns.
  --weight [imports|calls]        dsm view: cell value, edge presence
                                  (imports) or call_count (calls).
  --focus TEXT                    dsm view: qualname to focus on; keeps focus
                                  + its N-hop neighborhood.
  --focus-depth INTEGER           dsm view: hop count for --focus.
  --package TEXT                  dsm view: keep only modules whose qualname
                                  starts with this prefix.

content.text:
Floorplan has little archy should copy as a feature, but the integration idea is worth pursuing.

## What Floorplan is

It's a Node plugin for Claude Code and Codex, MIT, about 1.2k stars, at v0.6.1. A scan script parses imports, endpoints and web requests in many languages. The agent then writes `architecture.json`, which names the parts of the app and assigns files to them by glob. The agent also describes every file. The result is an interactive plain-English map, aimed at people who build with AI and don't read the code.

Its extras are a "Health" check for secrets and open endpoints, "Recent work" highlighting, screens, flows, an Ask bar, and blueprints from a PRD.

## Features to mirror

I ran these against the anti-theater test ("what does a user do differently because of this?") and WHAT_DIDNT_WORK. None is a clear yes.

| Floorplan feature | Verdict for archy |
|---|---|
| Health check (secrets, open Supabase/Firebase, unauthenticated endpoints) | **No.** It's a security scanner. The axis review already rejected "complete-codebase-health sensor" drift, and better tools own that niche. |
| Plain-English names and descriptions | **No.** It needs an LLM, and archy is a deterministic sensor. |
| Interactive zoomable node-link map | **No.** `SPEC_VISUALIZATION.md` rejects the generic graph ("pretty, low-signal"), and `archy render` deliberately has no `graph` view. |
| Recent work (cards the AI just changed, plus why) | **Mostly covered.** `affected` and `diff` already do the mechanical half. The "why" half is narrative, so it's not archy's job. |
| Blueprint from a PRD | **No.** It's greenfield and LLM-driven. |
| Typed edge kinds (http, queue, event, data) | **Maybe, later.** `SPEC_TYPED_CONNECTORS_AND_CONFORMANCE.md` already covers typing edges. Request-to-endpoint matching across repos would be a new capability for archy, but it needs a concrete consumer first. |
| `query.mjs find/show/path/overview` for agents | **Already covered.** The archy MCP tools do this. |
| Declared `ignore`, `include` and `annotations` with a `hotspot` tag | **Already covered.** archy has `exclude:` and `hotspots`. |

My honest answer is that I wouldn't file a mirror-this ticket. It would be a seventh "push a fact at the user" idea with no reason it differs from the earlier ones.

## Integration: archy as Floorplan's input

This looks more promising. Floorplan's weak spot is that the AI invents the structure and the scan is "pattern matching, not a compiler". archy computes things Floorplan can't:

1. **Seed `architecture.json` nodes from archy's output.**
   - The nodes come from `layers:` in `archy.yaml`, or from the community detection behind `dsm --group community`.
   - Each node's `paths` and `kind` would be derived from them, not guessed by the agent.
   - This targets Floorplan's "Unassigned" problem and the unstable part choices.
   - archy's choice is deterministic, so rebuilds wouldn't reshuffle the parts.
2. **Feed `annotations` with archy's signals.**
   - `{path, note, tags:["hotspot"]}` is a first-class Floorplan field.
   - archy could supply the hotspots (complexity x churn) and cycle (SCC) members.
   - It could also supply the high edit-risk modules, which is archy's unique signal.
   - The agent currently picks these by gut feel.
3. **Cross-check imports.** archy's resolved Python import graph is stricter than Floorplan's extractor. A diff between the two would show edges Floorplan misses.
4. **Keep the rules and the map in sync.** Floorplan draws what exists, and archy enforces what's allowed. Rules violations could show up as red edges on the map.

Implementation could be an `archy export --format floorplan` command, or just a recipe in `skills/archy/SKILL.md`. I'd start with the recipe, since it costs nothing and shows whether anyone uses it. `AGENTS.md` and usage data (under 20 real users) argue against building a command first.

## Caveats

- Floorplan is JavaScript-first and archy is Python-only, so the overlap is Python repos. Floorplan covers a dozen languages.
- I haven't run Floorplan or verified the quality of its Python extraction. That's the claim integration idea 3 depends on, and a one-repo comparison would settle it.
- The comparison table in Floorplan's README names Archify and Understand Anything but not archy.

## Next step

If you want one, the cheapest test is a spike. Run `archy hotspots` and community output through a hand-built `architecture.json` for archy's own repo, and see whether Floorplan's map improves. I wouldn't file anything before that.

# archy's own layer rules - enforced in CI via `archy check .`.
#
# The intent is a pure dependency tree:
#   parser  →  (nothing internal)
#   graph   →  parser
#   policy  →  graph
#   cli     →  parser, graph, policy
#
# Lower layers must not depend on higher ones.

layers:
  parser:
    modules:
      - "archy.parser"
  graph:
    modules:
      - "archy.graph"
      - "archy.cycles"
      - "archy.score"
      - "archy.history"
      - "archy.trend"
  policy:
    modules:
      - "archy.layers"
  cli:
    modules:
      - "archy.cli"
      - "archy.mcp"
      - "archy.scan_config"

forbid:
  - {from: parser, to: graph}
  - {from: parser, to: policy}
  - {from: parser, to: cli}
  - {from: graph,  to: policy}
  - {from: graph,  to: cli}
  - {from: policy, to: cli}

# Directories archy must not descend into -- all hold vendored external git
# clones created by the bench harness, gitignored and absent in CI:
#   replay_cache/ -- `bench/inloop_prevalence.py` checkouts at arbitrary commits
#   repo_cache/   -- `bench/run.py` clone cache (moved in-repo in #212)
#   cache/        -- misc bench scratch
# Scoring them pollutes archy's self-score and spins for minutes on the ~40k
# vendored `.py` files, and races the harness's concurrent `git checkout`s
# (FileNotFoundError on files that vanish mid-scan). Matched by basename, so any
# nested copy is skipped. Harmless in CI, where the directories do not exist.
exclude:
  - replay_cache
  - repo_cache
  - cache
  # Sample source trees for the benches, not archy code. `conduit_clean/violating`
  # deliberately contains an upward import, which forms a genuine 3-module cycle
  # (routes -> services -> repositories -> routes). archy's own `cycles --strict`
  # CI gate found it immediately, which is the gate working correctly on a tree
  # that is supposed to be broken.
  - fixtures

content.text:
I ran Floorplan on a copy of archy, once as Floorplan is designed to work and once with archy's output feeding it. Your repo is untouched; `git status` shows only the two untracked dirs it already had. Floorplan was never installed as a plugin. I ran its `scan.mjs` and `build.mjs` directly, acting as the agent that writes `architecture.json`.

## Evaluating Floorplan on archy

- **The mechanical scan is good.** In a few seconds it found 190 code files and 351 import edges, plus the external packages and hosts.
- **Its import edges agree with archy's.** I compared its 351 file-to-file edges with archy's 322 internal edges.
  - 320 are shared.
  - The 2 edges only archy sees are `from archy.install import <submodule>`; Floorplan links to the package `__init__` instead. This is a small precision win for archy.
  - The 31 edges only Floorplan sees are mostly `bench/` scripts importing each other, which archy doesn't resolve.
  - So "archy improves Floorplan's imports" is mostly false for Python.
- **The map is only as good as the AI's `architecture.json`.**
  - The part names and descriptions are all generated, and the app tells you so ("190 files still use generated names").
  - Floorplan's Health check found one thing, "3 files are very large". `archy hotspots` already flags the same `cli.py`, `mcp.py` and `test_mcp.py`.
- **The glob paths for `Dockerfile`, `.github/**` and `action.yml` matched nothing.** Floorplan only maps code files by default, so non-code files need `include`.
- **The Ask bar didn't work for me.** It needs the Claude Code CLI and a local server, and I didn't set that up.
- **My screenshot of the seeded map is invalid.** It was captured mid-animation, so I'm not drawing any visual conclusion from it.

## Spike: archy feeding Floorplan

- **Hotspot annotations worked mechanically.** 8 files from `archy hotspots` came through as hotspot-tagged cards, 15 in the graph.
- **Seeding the parts from `dsm --group community` made the map worse for a human.**
  - Within-part edges went from 43% (my hand-drawn parts) to 74%. I wouldn't count that as evidence, because community detection maximizes that number by construction.
  - The first community is a 17-module, 10k-line blob holding `cli`, `mcp`, `score`, `cycles` and `diff`.
  - Run over the whole repo, the communities also mixed tests and bench scripts in with source.
  - A human would not name that part "Commands and scoring core". The generic names I gave the communities show the same problem.
- **So `architecture.json` from archy is not a win.** It's neither better nor easier to explain than the agent's own grouping.

## What archy could mirror

- **Nothing about Floorplan's map or its scoring.** The Health check, plain-English names, blueprints and the interactive map fail the anti-theater gate or are already rejected in `SPEC_VISUALIZATION.md`. The "unassigned %" idea is already covered, since `archy check` reports layer coverage.
- **One cheap item: a trust page.** Floorplan has an "Is it safe to install?" page that lists:
  - everything it does on your machine
  - a test that checks it makes no hook, MCP or network calls
  - per-release file checksums

  archy is an MCP server that edits agent config files, and `SECURITY.md` has only two network lines. My search found no ticket for this. It's docs plus a test, so I'd file it.
- **A side finding about archy itself.** `archy check` reports that `archy.yaml` governs only 10 of 48 modules (21%). It also says the 6 forbid rules can't be verified at that coverage. That's worth fixing independently of Floorplan.

## Recommendation

Skip the `export --format floorplan` command and keep only the hotspot-annotation recipe in `skills/archy/SKILL.md`; the community seeding isn't worth shipping.

Do you want me to file the trust-page ticket and the `archy.yaml` coverage ticket? The artifacts are in the scratchpad: `armA/`, `armB/`, and `shotA.png` (the valid screenshot).

content.content:
Closes #388, #415, #416, #422. Batch 2 of the hygiene sweep, and unlike #469 this one touches production code.

## Why the suite passing proves nothing here

A behaviour-preserving refactor passes the test suite **by construction**. "1,247 tests green" is the weakest possible evidence for this PR, so every change was mutation-checked against its own subject instead.

That turned out to matter more than expected.

## A bug I introduced and caught

My first #422 edit asserted-and-exited *after* doing its replacements but *before* writing the file. The helper landed; the two call sites did not. **The suite stayed green because the helper was dead code.**

Mutation testing is what exposed it: hardcoding every knob inside the helper changed nothing, which is not a plausible result for live code. Reading the diff would not have caught it — the helper is right there and looks correct.

## The coverage hole that surfaced

With the helper actually wired, four of its six knobs could each be hardcoded and all 132 CLI tests stayed green:

| knob | covered before? |
|---|---|

**Discovery.** `archy check` walks PATH upward to find `archy.yaml` unless `--config` is given. Exits 1 on violation.

**Coverage.** Every `check` reports how much of your code the rules actually reach, on a pass as well as a failure:

```console
$ archy check .
# No layer violations (config: /path/to/archy/archy.yaml).
#   layer coverage: 10 of 48 modules (21%), 20 of 136 internal edges (15%); 38 module(s) match no layer (`archy check --show-unlayered`)
#   116 scanned module(s) sit outside every declared root package and are not counted above
#   6 forbid rules declared, but this check governs too little of the graph to verify them.
#   `archy check --contracts` evaluates them transitively via import-linter, which sees paths a direct-edge check cannot.
```

That line exists because **a rule set that cannot fire is indistinguishable from a clean codebase**: without it, a config governing 14% of your import edges prints the same "No layer violations" as one governing all of them. The edge percentage is the one to watch, since a config can put most module

----
archy.layers
archy.parser
...

$ uv run archy cycles .
# No cycles found (min_size=2).

$ uv run archy check .
# No layer violations (config: /Users/.../archy/archy.yaml).
#   layer coverage: 10 of 48 modules (21%), 20 of 136 internal edges (15%); 38 module(s) match no layer (`archy check --show-unlayered`)
```

The CI step (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) makes any layer-crossing PR fail
fast, so AI-assisted refactors can't quietly invert the dependency tree.

## Problem

`.importlinter` in the repo root is a hand-maintained mirror of `archy.yaml`'s forbid rules from the original four-layer config (#34). It has drifted: it puts `archy.diff` and `archy.impact` in the graph layer, but they sit above the policy layer. ```
# contracts: 2 kept, 1 broken (48 modules, 135 imports)
X  graph layer must not reach policy/cli layers
    archy.diff -> archy.layers
      via archy.diff -> archy.ratchet -> archy.layers
```

That is a false alarm: `diff` is an analysis module and may import `layers`. It is not run in CI (only `archy check` and `archy cycles --strict` are), so nothing flags the drift.

Found while working on #686, which layers every module in `archy.yaml`. With `.importlinter` set aside, the contracts derived from the new `archy.yaml` give 26 kept, 0 broken.

## Options

1. Delete `.importlinter` so the contracts derive from `archy.yaml` (one source of truth). The derived path warns it is "a best-effort fallback"; fine here since there are no `ignore_imports`.
2. Regenerate `.importlinter` from the new layers and add a test or CI step that fails when the two disagree.

Either way, decide whether `archy check . --contracts` should become a CI step, since otherwise the transitive rules can drift again unnoticed.

## Acceptance

`archy check . --contracts` on this repo reports no broken contracts and is correct about every contract it lists.

# DeepWork Review

Run automated code reviews on the current branch based on `.deepreview` config files.

## Routing — Check Before Proceeding

**STOP and redirect** if either of these applies:

- User wants to **configure, create, or modify** review rules (e.g., "add a security review", "set up reviews for our API layer") → use the `configure_reviews` skill instead

## Pre-flight — Verify Agent Availability

Before running reviews, check that the `deepwork:reviewer` agent is available. If it does not appear in the agents list (i.e., the Agent tool does not list `deepwork:reviewer` as a valid `subagent_type`), **STOP** and tell the user:

> The `deepwork:reviewer` agent is not available. Please run `/reload-plugins` to pick up the latest plugin updates, then try again.

Do not proceed with reviews until the agent is available.

## How to Run

1. Call the `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` tool directly:
   - **No arguments** to review the current branch's changes (auto-detects via git diff against the main branch).
   - **With `files`** to review only specific files: `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions(files=["src/app.py", "src/lib.py"])`. When provided, only reviews whose include/exclude patterns match the given files will be returned. Use this when the user asks to review a particular file or set of files rather than the whole branch.
   - **If the result says no rules are configured**: Ask the user if they'd like to auto-discover and set up rules. If yes, invoke the `/deepwork` skill with the `deepwork_reviews` job's `discover_rules` workflow. Stop here — do not proceed with running reviews if there are no rules.
2. The output will list review tasks to invoke in parallel. Each task has `description`, `subagent_type`, and `prompt` fields — these map directly to the Agent tool parameters. Launch all of them as parallel agents.
3. **While review agents run**, check for a changelog and open PR (see below).
4. Collect the results from all review agents.

## Changelog & PR Description Check

Run this concurrently with the review agents (step 2 above) — don't wait for reviews to finish first.

1. Check if the project has a changelog file (e.g., `CHANGELOG.md`, `CHANGELOG`, `CHANGES.md`).
2. If a changelog exists and there are commits on the current branch beyond the main branch:
   - Read the changelog and the branch's commit log (`git log main..HEAD --oneline`).
   - Verify the changelog's unreleased/current section accurately reflects what the branch does. If entries are missing, outdated, or inaccurate, update the changelog.
3. If a PR is open for the current branch (check with `gh pr view`):
   - If you updated the changelog, also verify the PR description matches. Update it with `gh pr edit` if needed.
   - If the changelog was already accurate, skip the PR description check.

## Acting on Results

For each finding from the review agents:

- **Obviously good changes with no downsides** (e.g., fixing a typo, removing an unused import, adding a missing null check): make the change immediately without asking. When in doubt, ask.
- **Everything else** (refactors, style changes, architectural suggestions, anything with trade-offs):
  1. Use AskUserQuestion to ask the user about each finding **individually**. Do not group issues together unless they are the same issue occurring in multiple files; otherwise, use AskUserQuestion to ask about each issue separately. This lets the user make separate decisions on each item.
  2. For each question, provide several concrete fix approaches as options when there are reasonable alternatives (e.g., "Update the spec to match the code" vs "Update the code to match the spec" vs "Skip").
  3. If a finding seems minor or debatable, include an option to suppress that error in the future — such as a clarification to the rule if it is too narrow, or a comment on the offending content if comments work in that context.
  4. Be concise — quote the key finding, don't dump the full review.

When a finding is dismissed (user chooses "Skip" or you determine it's not actionable for this PR), call `mcp__deepwork__mark_review_as_passed` with the review's ID so it won't re-run on subsequent iterations.

## Iterate

After making any changes:

1. Call `mcp__deepwork__get_review_instructions` with `files` set to **only the files you edited** during this iteration. This scopes the re-review to your changes rather than re-reviewing the entire branch.
2. Repeat the cycle (run → act on results → run again) until a clean run — one where all review agents return no findings, or all remaining findings have been explicitly skipped by the user.
3. On subsequent runs, you only need to re-run tasks that had findings last time — skip tasks that were clean.
